newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Body of slain IRA suspect arrives in Ireland. [CORRECTED 21:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Body of slain IRA suspect arrives in Ireland. [CORRECTED 21:45 GMT]

text.p: The body of a suspected IRA activist shot dead by police in a London raid arrived in Ireland on Wednesday for what his parents hope will be a funeral without guerrilla or political trappings.
The coffin carrying Diarmuid O'Neill, 27, was flown into Cork airport accompanied by his father and mother, Eoghan and Theresa, and his brother Shane and sister Siobhan.

Armed police searched the airport and grounds before the plane carrying the coffin from London arrived in Cork, southern Ireland's main city, to be taken to the O'Neill's family home in the nearby village of Timoleague.
The O'Neill family invited cameramen and television crews to a photo-call in their family home in Timoleague, a small cottage overlooking a picturesque estuary.
But they were overwhelmed by the number of reporters who gathered at the front gate.

Family member John Dawson emerged briefly from the cottage with a statement which said: "We are unable to give an interview or pose for photographs. We need time to grieve for Diarmuid. Thank you for your understanding at this difficult time."
(Corrects to make clear family member John Dawson issued the statement not brother Shane O'Neill.)
The family bought the cottage as a holiday home but decided to return from Britain and live there permanently this year.
Diarmuid O'Neill was brought up in London.
The family has been in contact with police to ensure that the ceremony is not turned into a publicity coup for the IRA or its Sinn Fein political wing, sources close to the family said.
The IRA usually gives its "volunteers" a hero's send-off with a volley of shots fired over a coffin draped with the Irish tricolour national flag carried by men in paramilitary unform.

O'Neill was gunned down last week, apparently unarmed, when police raided a London house and found tonnes of explosive, automatic weapons and other equipement they said was to have been used by an Irish Republican Army (IRA) cell.

His death has provoked allegations from Irish Republican sympathisers in Britain and elsehwere that police were operating a "shoot-to-kill-policy" against the IRA, which has fought British rule of Northern Ireland for 25 years.
Four men arrrested in the raid are in jail awaiting trial on charges of arms possession in connection with the disovery of tonnes of explosive and several automatic weapons.

The discovery led to a crisis in the Northern Ireland peace process when Protestant Loyalist militia battling to maintain British rule of Northern Ireland hinted that they would break a two-year truce unless the IRA silenced its own weapons.
